title: Design a Real-Time Collaborative Editor (Google Docs)
prompt: Design a Google-Docs-style real-time collaborative editor: many users edit the same document simultaneously, everyone sees each other's changes within a fraction of a second, edits never get lost, and everyone converges to the same final document. Cover the concurrency-control model, the sync protocol, and presence.
blurb: The convergence problem — Operational Transformation vs CRDTs, ordering concurrent edits so everyone ends up identical, plus presence, cursors, and offline.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (concurrent edit, live sync, cursors/presence, history/undo, offline) from non-functional (convergence/consistency, low latency, no lost edits, availability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about concurrent editors per doc, latency target, offline support, rich text vs plain, undo semantics, document size.

rubric.label: Concurrency-control model
rubric.description: OT vs CRDT: how concurrent edits are reconciled, why last-write-wins on the whole doc is wrong, guaranteeing convergence and intention preservation.

rubric.label: OT / CRDT depth
rubric.description: For OT: transform functions, central server ordering, TP1/TP2. For CRDT: unique positional identifiers, tombstones, commutative merges, metadata overhead.

rubric.label: Sync protocol
rubric.description: Client-server op exchange over websockets, versioning/revision numbers, acknowledgements, rebasing client ops against server history, buffering unacked ops.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Clients <-> websocket gateway <-> per-document server/actor applying and broadcasting ops -> op log + snapshots persisted; presence channel.

rubric.label: Consistency & convergence
rubric.description: Guarantees all replicas converge; ordering, causality, and how history/undo/redo stay coherent across users.

rubric.label: Presence & offline
rubric.description: Live cursors/selections/awareness, ephemeral vs durable state, and reconciling edits made while offline on reconnect.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Routing all editors of one doc to one authority (single-writer per doc), sharding docs across servers, hot documents, op-log compaction/snapshots.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: The per-document server as a serialization point, unbounded op-log growth, large documents, many cursors broadcasting.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Op apply latency, convergence/divergence detection, unacked-op backlog, presence channel load, snapshot lag.

functional_requirements: Multiple users edit one document concurrently with live updates
All users converge to an identical document
Live cursors, selections, and presence (who's here)
nonfunctional_requirements: No lost edits; strong eventual convergence
Highly available editing; durable document + history
Scales to many docs and dozens of concurrent editors per doc
Intention preservation (edits mean what the user intended after merge)
clarifying_questions: Max concurrent editors per document, and total docs?
Latency target for seeing others' edits?
Plain text or rich text / structured content?
Is offline editing a first-class requirement?
How large can a single document get?
qualifying_questions: Is a central authority per document acceptable, or must it be peer-to-peer/decentralized?
How long must full edit history be retained?
Is intention preservation (not just convergence) required for rich text?

estimations.traffic: Millions of docs, but concurrency is per-doc; a hot doc might have 50 editors each producing a few ops/sec -> a few hundred ops/sec per hot doc, broadcast to all editors.
estimations.oplog: A long-lived doc accrues huge op history; compact with periodic snapshots (snapshot + tail of ops) so load/replay is bounded.
estimations.presence: Cursor/selection updates are high-frequency but ephemeral — coalesce and send at ~10Hz, not per keystroke.
estimations.fanout: Each op fans out to (editors-1) clients; a 50-editor doc at 200 ops/s is ~10K messages/s on that doc's channel.

core_components: Concurrency engine (OT transform or CRDT merge)
data_model: ops(doc_id, revision, author, op, parent_revision, ts) — ordered op log
presence(doc_id, user_id, cursor, selection, last_seen) — ephemeral
api_design: WS connect doc -> server sends snapshot + revision
client -> { op, baseRevision }; server transforms/merges, assigns revision, acks + broadcasts
server -> { op, revision } to all other editors
presence: { cursor, selection } coalesced, broadcast ephemerally
reference.high_level_design: All editors of a document connect (via websocket gateways) to a single per-document authority (an actor/process that owns that doc), so there is one serialization point that assigns a total order of revisions. A client applies edits locally for responsiveness and sends each op tagged with the revision it was based on. The server transforms (OT) or merges (CRDT) the incoming op against any ops it has accepted since that base, assigns the next revision, appends to the op log, acks the sender, and broadcasts the transformed op to other editors, who transform their own in-flight ops against it. Presence (cursors/selections) rides a separate ephemeral channel. The op log is periodically compacted into snapshots to bound replay and storage. On reconnect after offline editing, the client rebases its buffered ops against the server's newer history before they're accepted.

deep_dives.probe: Two users insert text at the same position simultaneously. Walk through how OT transforms the operations vs how a CRDT assigns positional identifiers so both converge — and why naive last-write-wins on the document is wrong.
OT vs CRDT: what does OT need from a central server (ordering, transform correctness / TP1-TP2), and what does a CRDT pay in per-character metadata and tombstones? When would you choose each?
How does a client reconcile its optimistically-applied local ops when the server acks a different revision order — buffering unacked ops and rebasing? What revision/versioning scheme do you use?
Why route all editors of a doc to one authority, and how do you fail over that authority without losing ops or double-applying? What happens to in-flight ops during failover?
The op log grows without bound and undo/history must work. How do you snapshot/compact while keeping undo/redo and version history coherent?

Documents and ops live in a datastore. Search, activity feeds, and analytics need to know about edits. How do you propagate changes out — change data capture / Debezium off the op/document store, or emitting domain events on commit?

followup_bank.question: How do you guarantee transform correctness (TP1/TP2) and intention preservation, and why does OT typically need a central server?
What's the per-character metadata and tombstone cost of your CRDT, and how do you garbage-collect tombstones without breaking convergence?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cache or redis or presence
followup_bank.question: Presence is ephemeral and high-frequency — what's its TTL/eviction, and how do you avoid a stampede/broadcast storm when a hot doc reconnects many clients at once?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or postgres or sql or oplog
followup_bank.question: How do you stream document/op changes to search, activity feeds, and analytics — CDC/Debezium off the store vs dual writes? And how do snapshots bound the op log?
How do all editors of one doc get routed to the same per-document authority, and how does failover of that authority avoid losing or double-applying in-flight ops?

scaling: Single-writer authority per document; shard documents across servers by doc_id
Route by doc so all editors converge on one serialization point
Compact op logs into periodic snapshots (snapshot + op tail)
Separate ephemeral presence channel; coalesce cursor updates
Horizontal websocket gateways with a session registry keyed by doc
bottlenecks: Per-document authority as the serialization point / hot-doc limit
Presence broadcast storms on very active docs
tradeoffs: OT (compact ops, needs central server + correct transforms) vs CRDT (peer-friendly, metadata/tombstone overhead)
Optimistic local apply (responsive, needs rebasing) vs server-confirmed (simpler, laggy)
Frequent snapshots (fast load, write cost) vs infrequent (cheap, slow replay)
Central authority (simple convergence) vs decentralized (available offline, harder to reason about)
alternative_solutions: OT with a central document server (Google-Docs-style)
Locking / section-level check-out (avoids merge, poor UX for prose)
observability: Divergence detection (checksum/hash of converged state across clients)
Presence channel message rate per doc
security: Per-document ACLs enforced on connect and per op
Sanitize/validate ops (no privilege escalation via crafted ops)
Rate-limit ops per client to prevent abuse
Audit trail via the op log; encryption in transit and at rest
reference.reference_answer: A staff-level answer frames the crux as convergence of concurrent edits and chooses a concurrency-control model deliberately: OT with a central per-document authority that assigns a total order and transforms ops (addressing TP1/TP2 and intention preservation), or a CRDT with unique positional ids and tombstones for offline/P2P, naming each model's costs. It applies edits optimistically on the client and rebases unacked ops against server-assigned revisions, routes all editors of a doc to one serialization authority with a clear failover story, compacts the op log via snapshots, and runs presence on a separate ephemeral channel. It streams op/document changes to search and analytics via CDC, and identifies the per-doc authority and op-log growth as the main bottlenecks.

interviewer_notes: This is a staff-level question; the whole interview lives or dies on the concurrency-control model. Do not accept 'sync the text' or whole-document last-write-wins — force a concrete story for two simultaneous inserts at the same position, and make them commit to OT or CRDT and defend it (transform correctness/TP1-TP2 for OT; positional ids and tombstone GC for CRDT). Probe the sync protocol: optimistic local apply plus rebasing unacked ops against server revisions. If they place an op/document store, hit the CDC/Debezium probe; if they mention presence/Redis, probe ephemeral TTL and reconnect broadcast storms. Reserve time for the single-writer authority and its failover, and for op-log compaction/snapshots keeping undo/history coherent.
